studies.title: Fast Models, Slow Evidence: A Paired and Self-Audited Evaluation of System-1 Decision Models for LLM Agent Harnesses
models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and other reference judges for selected controls

result_claims.claim: Original tool-selection accuracy is Jev 398/400 (99.5%) vs Laya 336/400 (84.0%).
Original routing accuracy is Jev 200/400 (50%) vs Laya 194/400 (48.5%).
After reversing choice criteria order, B tool selection changes 0/400 Jev and 76/400 Laya. F high-cardinality/multilingual single-choice intent classification changes 17/200 Jev and 106/200 Laya.

The A routing order variant also removes the original difficulty question, because build_flip_large.mjs retains only the first choice question. The aggregate 30.3% Laya / 1.8% Jev answer-change rates reproduce numerically but cannot be attributed solely to candidate order for A/ALL.
In the study's 540-case safety cascade at threshold 0.1, omitting the screen cost suggests 23.9% savings; including it leaves about 4.3%.
In the routing subset Jev has 184 errors among 375 answers with max option probability >=0.9; in tool selection it has 0 errors among 391 such answers.

limits: Independent work here reproduces arithmetic on historical public records; no model inference or present-day service validation.
Routing descriptions, clipped inputs and historical gold strongly limit generalization.
Confidence thresholds are workload-specific; some safety labels/controls are model-assisted.
Open benchmarks may be in training data; variants are correlated.

key_conditions.our_reanalysis: 1,000 choice cases: RouterBench 400; BFCL 400; BANKING77/MASSIVE 200, four saved response records each
key_conditions.score_semantics: Top-option probability; Laya's own confidence field uses a different scale and is not substituted in our measurements

studies.title: Evaluating and Benchmarking the System One Model Jev

result_claims.claim: Jev's pooled Choice ECE is 0.028; mean per-dataset ECE is 0.061. Three large datasets provide 63% of pooled answers.
UNFAIR-ToS micro-F1 rises from 0.499274 to 0.748166 after dev-only per-question threshold tuning, with no model change.
Main evaluation costs $9.15; whole study including pilot/additional analysis $9.40.

limits: Prompts were designed for Jev; not optimized for the open baselines.
No reasoning-enabled proprietary comparator and no repeated requests.
The suite contains no dedicated relevance-judgment task.
The public response dataset has a separate restrictive Jev Responses License; code MIT does not make all responses unrestricted.
We read implementation and aggregate results; we did not download/recompute all 346,009 responses.

key_conditions.sample: 346,009 requests across 37 public datasets; 22 Choice datasets contain 279,925 answers for pooled calibration.
key_conditions.thresholds: Per-question thresholds use 1,000 dev examples on four datasets, grid 0.02..0.98 in steps of .01, maximize F1 with ties closest to .5; evaluated unchanged on held-out split.

studies.title: JEV versus LLMs: Accuracy, Cost and Calibration on Seven Political Science Replications
models: Jev 1.13, commonly via OpenRouter; responses typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917
GPT-6 Luna through its generative Batch/API route, reasoning none
Qwen3.8-27B via OpenRouter/Parasail FP8, reasoning off

result_claims.claim: Jev has no consistent cost advantage over Luna Batch on these tasks; at synchronous Standard prices it is cheaper on six of seven.
Measured sequential Jev median latency spans 0.09–0.27 s vs Luna 0.75–1.04 s and Qwen 0.39–0.87 s.

Jev's choice probabilities calibrate better than Luna's first-answer-token probabilities in single-pass reading tasks, but not uniformly better than Qwen. Averaging both presentation orders narrows the difference.
The authors did not test the OpenAI Decisions endpoint released October 6.

limits: OpenAI's new Decisions API was not evaluated.
Name-only tasks may recall public benchmark labels seen during training.
Some original prompts unavailable; reconstructed framing prompts are not comparable with old published numbers.
Human raters disagree; F1 on first-item preference depends on presentation order.
Hosted Qwen cost is route-specific, not self-host total cost.

key_conditions.tasks: Seven prior political-science annotation/scaling replications plus additional calibration tasks. Includes text-reading tasks and name-only recall tasks, which have different constructs.
key_conditions.timings: 200 timed items per application, from the Netherlands on 2026-09-29/30; sequential median and concurrency-16 throughput.

studies.code_availability_limit: Paper/author post say scripts and responses are in a replication archive; no direct public archive URL was located in the inspected paper HTML or author post. Do not imply independent code/data reproduction.

studies.title: winnow — calibrated context sieve for Claude Code
models: Jev through TypeSafe (aggregate score files do not pin returned model version; README default jev-latest)
Claude Fable 5.1 as the labeler of the 97 decided 'hand' labels
Local jevlike trial on weak replay labels; lexical baseline

result_claims.claim: At p<0.1, strict wording hides 35 labeled blocks; 8/35 (~22.9%) are needed under the model-assisted labels. Structured wording hides 23, with 0 labeled-needed in that small sample.
Structured phrasing's population text reduction at threshold .1 is about 4.6%, despite its worse aggregate ECE than the default phrasing.
A local weakly trained model attains ECE 0.135 while AUROC is ~0.497: it effectively predicts the base rate and cannot usefully rank blocks.
Question wording, explicit examples and task reconstruction are adjustable inputs to an executable policy; uncertainty and error handling are implemented outside the model.

limits: Model-assisted labels and tiny human audit; no human-validated broad benchmark.
Weak reuse labels can mislabel in both directions; not a clean upper bound on regret.
Shadow mode cannot measure actual recall regret.
Current Claude Code hook behavior is version-dependent; installing the repository does not prove live integration.
We inspected code/results, did not install hooks or send private transcripts.

key_conditions.sample: 300 cases / 1,515 weak-labeled blocks from one developer's history. Probability-stratified sample of 100 blocks labeled by Claude: 47 needed,50 not needed,3 unsure.
key_conditions.label_warning: Despite names 'hand'/'blind hand labels', original DESIGN/WRITEUP and raw score note identify Claude as labeler. Later small human audit agreed poorly; not human ground truth.

studies.title: Evaluating System One Models for Agent Security Decisions: Reliability, Calibration, and Selective Automation
models: Specialized detectors, original parent controls, GPT-4.1/Qwen and five reasoning judges

result_claims.claim: Good global accuracy/calibration can coexist with confident mistakes concentrated in specific attack groups.

For Jev shipped probabilities on WAInject at 1% miss limit, symmetric selection chooses no automation; independent thresholds yield test coverage 108/1,612 (~6.70%), entirely automatic blocks and zero automatic allows.
A reviewer can both recover misses and introduce benign false alarms or share the first model's confident failures; error complementarity must be measured on the actual reviewed subset.

The source-selected policy code checks disjoint partition IDs, fits recalibration on development data and selects thresholds on selection data; unsupported probabilities do not become automatic allows.

limits: Rare-event error estimates have small independent sample counts; bootstrap is not a certification.
Some policy analyses are exploratory/retrospective despite held-out calculation.
Hosted versions change; public datasets may be contaminated and do not model adaptive attackers.
AgentHarm request harmfulness and WAInject attack-derived text are different positive events.
No current provider or live agent was tested by this research.

key_conditions.retrospective_limit: Repository explicitly states threshold-sensitivity completion/reanalysis followed initial test inspection; not a new prospective validation.

studies.title: Calibrated Decisions at Scale: Converting Police Crash Narratives into Probabilistic Crash Variables with a System One Model (Jev)
models: claude-fable-5-1 and gpt-5.6-sol for separate human-reference quality comparison

result_claims.claim: The actual full-coding stage costs $30.22 for 195,857 narratives, about $0.154 per 1,000. The $774 figure is an extrapolation to 5,018,080, not an executed full-corpus bill.

Published cost-model fit has ~170.7 base tokens +121.5 tokens/question; schema overhead dominates these short narratives. The paper reports an executed screen break-even pass-through fraction of 0.67.
Jev reaches F1 .908 against the weighted human reference yet fails multiple calibration checks; rare-event prevalence and discrete probability resolution matter.
Metric functions accept sampling weights; the review budget is defined over flagged records at target precision rather than all-record accuracy.
Frontier quality arms have no token accounting, so the separate frontier cost scenarios are not measured costs for those benchmarked arms.

limits: Single domain/state; not an all-purpose provider comparison.
Narrative reference evaluates what a narrative says, not what happened in the world.
Private underlying narratives/raw responses are not redistributed; only aggregate results and code inspected.
Do not infer universal calibration from model training labels or vendor claims.
README's broad whole-corpus language must be read against paper's actually executed sample sizes.

key_conditions.corpus: 5,018,080 available Texas narratives; actually screened 499,500 and fully coded 195,857. Population extrapolation uses the random stratum of 150,000.
key_conditions.human_reference: 2,416 usable variable–narrative consensus labels from a sampling design involving 400 narratives; these are not 2,416 distinct crash reports. Probability-stratified selection requires weights.

method: Source/code audit and independent arithmetic on historical public outputs; no new inference.
